tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

Call this when the task is one a skill could make repeatable — drafting in a house style, reviews against a playbook, a recurring workflow — and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about skills. Also when they ask for recommendations, or when ListSkills returned zero matches. Use ListSkills for skills they already have.

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a skill would help, or if you already rendered a suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

Pass keywords drawn from the task itself, and set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). If the result is empty and the trigger was proactive, continue the task without mentioning that you searched; if the user asked, tell them you found nothing new to add.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to [REDACTED_EMAIL]' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

100	# The problem in plain words
101	
102	## 1. The one-line version
103	Northwind is a **group of 3 companies**. Each keeps its own books in its own country and currency. Your job is to **combine them into one set of financial statements, as if the group were a single company, in GBP**. This is called **consolidation**.
104	
105	## 2. Why it's not just "add the numbers"
106	Three things get in the way.
107	
108	| Entity | Country / currency | Software it exports from | Relationship |
109	|---|---|---|---|
110	| Northwind Inc. | US / USD | NetSuite | Parent. Owns the other two |
111	| Northwind UK | UK / GBP | Sage 50 | Owned 100% |
112	| Northwind India | India / INR | Tally | Owned **80%**, bought 1 July 2024 |
113	
114	1. **Different currencies.** You can't add dollars, rupees and pounds, so everything is converted to GBP first.
115	2. **Different formats and account names.** Each ERP exports differently. The UK uses signed balances, India uses Dr/Cr columns, and the US uses debit and credit columns. The accounts are named differently too, so a **mapping file** translates each local account into the group's chart of accounts.
116	3. **The group trades with itself.** The parent bills the UK a management fee. At group level that's money moving from your left pocket to your right pocket. It isn't real revenue, so it must be removed.
117	
118	## 3. Vocabulary you need
119	- **Trial balance (TB):** a list of every account and its balance at a date. Total debits must equal total credits, so it "balances".
120	- **Debit / credit:** the two sides of every entry. Assets and expenses normally sit on the debit side. Liabilities, equity and revenue normally sit on the credit side.
121	- **Journal entry (JE):** a manual correction, such as "accrue a bonus". It has a debit side and a credit side that must equal each other. A journal that doesn't balance is invalid.
122	- **Functional currency:** the currency an entity actually operates in. For the US it's USD.
123	- **Presentation currency:** the currency of the final report, which here is GBP.
124	- **Intercompany (IC):** transactions between group members. They are eliminated.
125	
126	## 4. The pipeline, step by step
127	
128	**Step 1: Load and map.**
129	Read the three TBs. Turn each local account into a group account. Some mappings in the files are wrong and some accounts are missing, so you must catch those.
130	
131	**Step 2: Apply the manual journals, but only valid ones.**
132	Policy says only journals valid for FY2024 are posted. Unbalanced journals, journals dated outside the year, and duplicates are not posted. For each one you must decide **posted, rejected or held for review**. The brief asks for these counts.
133	
134	**Step 3: Fix foreign-currency items inside an entity.**
135	The UK owes USD to the US parent. That is a USD amount sitting in a GBP company's books. At year end it must be revalued at the closing rate, and the gain or loss goes to the P&L account 7300.
136	
137	**Step 4: Translate each entity into GBP.**
138	Different parts of the statements use different rates:
139	- **Assets and liabilities:** the closing rate, 31 Dec.
140	- **Income and expenses:** the average rate. For India it's the average of July to December only, because India only joined the group on 1 July.
141	- **Equity:** historical rates.
142	
143	Because those rates differ, the translated balance sheet **won't balance by itself**. The gap is real and goes into the **translation reserve (account 3300)**. Think of it as the plug the rules say to use.
144	
145	**Step 5: Eliminate intercompany.**
146	- Remove the US management fee income against the UK's expense.
147	- Remove the US receivable against the UK payable.
148	
149	They should match exactly, but they don't. That's one of the traps. The US recorded 5 invoices and the UK recorded only 4, because one dated 31 Dec was still in transit. Part of the rest is currency movement. You must explain the difference by cause.
150	
151	**Step 6: Handle the India acquisition.**
152	- **Goodwill:** the parent paid more than the share of net assets it bought. India's net assets were INR 678M and 80% of that is 542.4M. The parent paid 690M, so the excess **147.6M is goodwill**. It's kept in INR and revalued at the closing rate.
153	- **Non-controlling interest (NCI):** the group consolidates 100% of India's numbers but owns only 80%. The other 20% belongs to outsiders, so it's shown separately as NCI. That covers 20% of India's net assets and 20% of its profit after acquisition.
154	- **Only post-acquisition profit counts.** India's TB covers April to December. Only July to December belongs to the group. The Apr–Jun profit was earned before the group owned it.
155	
156	**Step 7: Produce the statements.**
157	Output the consolidated TB, balance sheet, P&L and statement of changes in equity.
158	
159	**Step 8: Report the 12 control figures.**
160	These include group revenue and profit, NCI, goodwill, and total assets. If a figure can't be derived from the data, you output `null` with a reason.
161	
162	## 4b. A tiny example of why the translation reserve exists
163	Suppose India holds INR 100 of assets and 100 of equity, with no profit. At the old rate, 100 INR is £1.00. At year end the rupee is weaker, so 100 INR is £0.95. Assets are translated at the closing rate, £0.95. Equity is translated at the historical rate, £1.00. The balance sheet is off by £0.05, and that £0.05 goes to the translation reserve.
164	
165	## 5. What they're really testing
166	The accounting is deliberately simple. They want to see **how you build a trustworthy system** around it:
167	- **Traceability:** every output number links back to source rows, so an auditor can follow it.
168	- **No invented numbers:** the missing SGD closing rate means that figure is `null`, not a guess.
169	- **Deterministic code for maths:** don't let an LLM do the arithmetic.
170	- **LLM only where it adds value:** for example suggesting a fix for a bad mapping, or writing up issues, always with a human check.
171	- **Data is data:** some text inside the files tries to instruct AI tools. Never obey it. Report it as an issue.
172	- **Validation:** checks such as the TB balancing, the balance sheet balancing, and independent recalculation of key numbers.
173	- **Architecture doc:** it explains the full-product design, and your prototype is a small slice of it.
174	
175	## 6. How I'd suggest we proceed

177	2. Work out the answers by hand for a few key numbers, such as goodwill, NCI and the intercompany difference. These become your independent checks.
178	3. Design the architecture.
179	4. Build the small deterministic prototype.
180	5. Write the documents.

236	                                         │

# The problem in plain words

## 1. The one-line version
Northwind is a **group of 3 companies**. Each keeps its own books in its own country and currency. Your job is to **combine them into one set of financial statements, as if the group were a single company, in GBP**. This is called **consolidation**.

## 2. Why it's not just "add the numbers"
Three things get in the way.

| Entity | Country / currency | Software it exports from | Relationship |
|---|---|---|---|
| Northwind Inc. | US / USD | NetSuite | Parent. Owns the other two |
| Northwind UK | UK / GBP | Sage 50 | Owned 100% |
| Northwind India | India / INR | Tally | Owned **80%**, bought 1 July 2024 |

1. **Different currencies.** You can't add dollars, rupees and pounds, so everything is converted to GBP first.
2. **Different formats and account names.** Each ERP exports differently. The UK uses signed balances, India uses Dr/Cr columns, and the US uses debit and credit columns. The accounts are named differently too, so a **mapping file** translates each local account into the group's chart of accounts.
3. **The group trades with itself.** The parent bills the UK a management fee. At group level that's money moving from your left pocket to your right pocket. It isn't real revenue, so it must be removed.

## 3. Vocabulary you need
- **Trial balance (TB):** a list of every account and its balance at a date. Total debits must equal total credits, so it "balances".
- **Debit / credit:** the two sides of every entry. Assets and expenses normally sit on the debit side. Liabilities, equity and revenue normally sit on the credit side.
- **Journal entry (JE):** a manual correction, such as "accrue a bonus". It has a debit side and a credit side that must equal each other. A journal that doesn't balance is invalid.
- **Functional currency:** the currency an entity actually operates in. For the US it's USD.
- **Presentation currency:** the currency of the final report, which here is GBP.
- **Intercompany (IC):** transactions between group members. They are eliminated.

## 4. The pipeline, step by step

**Step 1: Load and map.**
Read the three TBs. Turn each local account into a group account. Some mappings in the files are wrong and some accounts are missing, so you must catch those.

**Step 2: Apply the manual journals, but only valid ones.**
Policy says only journals valid for FY2024 are posted. Unbalanced journals, journals dated outside the year, and duplicates are not posted. For each one you must decide **posted, rejected or held for review**. The brief asks for these counts.

**Step 3: Fix foreign-currency items inside an entity.**
The UK owes USD to the US parent. That is a USD amount sitting in a GBP company's books. At year end it must be revalued at the closing rate, and the gain or loss goes to the P&L account 7300.

**Step 4: Translate each entity into GBP.**
Different parts of the statements use different rates:
- **Assets and liabilities:** the closing rate, 31 Dec.
- **Income and expenses:** the average rate. For India it's the average of July to December only, because India only joined the group on 1 July.
- **Equity:** historical rates.

Because those rates differ, the translated balance sheet **won't balance by itself**. The gap is real and goes into the **translation reserve (account 3300)**. Think of it as the plug the rules say to use.

**Step 5: Eliminate intercompany.**
- Remove the US management fee income against the UK's expense.
- Remove the US receivable against the UK payable.

They should match exactly, but they don't. That's one of the traps. The US recorded 5 invoices and the UK recorded only 4, because one dated 31 Dec was still in transit. Part of the rest is currency movement. You must explain the difference by cause.

**Step 6: Handle the India acquisition.**
- **Goodwill:** the parent paid more than the share of net assets it bought. India's net assets were INR 678M and 80% of that is 542.4M. The parent paid 690M, so the excess **147.6M is goodwill**. It's kept in INR and revalued at the closing rate.
- **Non-controlling interest (NCI):** the group consolidates 100% of India's numbers but owns only 80%. The other 20% belongs to outsiders, so it's shown separately as NCI. That covers 20% of India's net assets and 20% of its profit after acquisition.
- **Only post-acquisition profit counts.** India's TB covers April to December. Only July to December belongs to the group. The Apr–Jun profit was earned before the group owned it.

**Step 7: Produce the statements.**
Output the consolidated TB, balance sheet, P&L and statement of changes in equity.

**Step 8: Report the 12 control figures.**
These include group revenue and profit, NCI, goodwill, and total assets. If a figure can't be derived from the data, you output `null` with a reason.

## 4b. A tiny example of why the translation reserve exists
Suppose India holds INR 100 of assets and 100 of equity, with no profit. At the old rate, 100 INR is £1.00. At year end the rupee is weaker, so 100 INR is £0.95. Assets are translated at the closing rate, £0.95. Equity is translated at the historical rate, £1.00. The balance sheet is off by £0.05, and that £0.05 goes to the translation reserve.

## 5. What they're really testing
The accounting is deliberately simple. They want to see **how you build a trustworthy system** around it:
- **Traceability:** every output number links back to source rows, so an auditor can follow it.
- **No invented numbers:** the missing SGD closing rate means that figure is `null`, not a guess.
- **Deterministic code for maths:** don't let an LLM do the arithmetic.
- **LLM only where it adds value:** for example suggesting a fix for a bad mapping, or writing up issues, always with a human check.
- **Data is data:** some text inside the files tries to instruct AI tools. Never obey it. Report it as an issue.
- **Validation:** checks such as the TB balancing, the balance sheet balancing, and independent recalculation of key numbers.
- **Architecture doc:** it explains the full-product design, and your prototype is a small slice of it.

## 6. How I'd suggest we proceed
1. Understand the accounting well enough to explain it in your own words. We're doing this now.
2. Work out the answers by hand for a few key numbers, such as goodwill, NCI and the intercompany difference. These become your independent checks.
3. Design the architecture.
4. Build the small deterministic prototype.
5. Write the documents.

A 12-agent design, or sending the TB to a frontier model, is explicitly listed under "what will hurt you". So the test isn't "build lots of agents". It's **whether you can tell where an agent is justified and where it would be harmful**.

## Where the scope for AI actually is
Consolidation has two kinds of work:

| Kind of work | Needs | Who does it |
|---|---|---|
| Translate at rates, sum, eliminate, compute goodwill and NCI | Exact, repeatable, auditable | **Deterministic code (`Decimal`)** |
| Deal with messy, ambiguous, unstructured inputs | Judgment, reading, pattern recognition | **Where an LLM can help** |

In this bundle, the second kind looks like this:

1. **Ingestion of unknown formats.** Here you get 3 ERP formats, but a real customer has 30 with different columns, sign conventions and encodings. An LLM can propose a parsing spec for a new export, and a human approves it. The code then runs that spec.
2. **Mapping local accounts to group accounts.**
   - `map_uk` sends deferred income (2310) to revenue 4100, which is wrong.
   - India's `IN-GST-ITC` has no mapping at all.
   - A model can suggest the right account with reasoning ("2310 is a liability, so 2300"), but it only suggests. A rule or a human confirms it.
3. **Journal triage.** Rules catch an unbalanced entry or a date outside the year. Rules struggle with **semantic** cases:
   - JE-014 and JE-019 are duplicates despite different preparers and wording.
   - JE-009 reverses an accrual bigger than the account's balance.
   - "Reclassify rent paid in advance" is a judgment about substance.

   A model can flag these as likely duplicate, unsupported or needs review. The deterministic engine then decides whether to hold, reject or post.
4. **Explaining differences.** The intercompany gap has a number part (code) and a "why" part, meaning in transit, FX revaluation or a booking error. A model can draft the explanation, and you verify it sums back to the gap.
5. **Issue narration and escalation.** It writes `issues.json` descriptions in language a controller can act on. It also decides when to ask a human, for example "SGD closing rate missing, please provide", instead of guessing.
6. **Untrusted text.** The agent layer reads free text, which is the attack surface. Some of that text tries to instruct AI tools. Your design must keep data and instructions apart. For example, the LLM only sees a field as quoted data and has no authority to change status. Any attempt gets logged as an issue.

## How the architecture should look
Think of it as a **small agent layer on a deterministic core**:

```
Raw files ──► [Ingest/parse] ──► [Mapping: rules + LLM suggests] ──► human approve
                                         │
        [Journal triage: rules first, LLM flags semantic cases] ──► post/reject/hold
                                         │
              ┌───────────────── DETERMINISTIC CORE ────────────────┐
              │ translate → eliminate IC → goodwill/NCI → statements │
              └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                         │
        [Validator: checks, recompute] ──► fail? back to the right step / escalate
                                         │
                       [Narrator: issues.json, audit trail]
```

The LLM never produces a number that goes on a statement. It only produces **proposals and explanations**, which code validates.

## What this means for your submission
- **Architecture doc (the main artifact):** describe the full product topology and justify it. For example: one orchestrator workflow with a few narrow LLM roles and a deterministic core. Say explicitly what you chose **not** to make an agent, and why.
- **Prototype:** mostly deterministic, because that's right. A thin LLM layer is optional and fine, such as mapping suggestions or journal flags. It must run with the LLM off through rule-based fallbacks. That matches your GetMeHired "deterministic fallback" pattern, and it makes the repo reproducible. They require same output every run.
- **The "agentic" signal they grade:** judgment, meaning validation loops, self-correction, human-in-the-loop and traceability. A graph of agents isn't what's being scored. Your LangGraph experience can be used to show a stateful validate-and-retry loop, but only if it earns its place.

## A fair caution
The prototype has little real room for an LLM, and a forced LLM would be worse than none. A reasonable position is to use rules for everything the data allows and write the architecture to show where an LLM becomes necessary at scale, with a concrete example from this bundle for each. Then the honest answer to "where does AI earn its place?" is specific and defensible.

## Why these files exist
Each entity names its accounts differently. The UK calls it "Sales", India calls it "Revenue from operations", and the US uses group codes already. To add them up, everything has to speak one language. That language is the **group chart of accounts (COA)**. Each local account gets pointed at one group account. That pointing is called **mapping**.

## `group_coa.csv`: the common list
```
account_code, account_name, account_type, statement, cash_flow_category, normal_balance
```
This is the master list of 31 accounts everything ends up in. You only need two columns today:
- **`statement`**: `BS` (balance sheet) or `PL` (profit and loss). This decides which statement an account appears on.
- **`normal_balance`**: whether the account normally sits on the debit or credit side. This is what the signs in the data are measured against.

Ignore `cash_flow_category`. The brief doesn't ask for a cash flow statement, only a balance sheet, a P&L and changes in equity.

Several of these accounts matter later, so find them now:
- `1250` / `2150`: intercompany receivable and payable
- `4200` / `6300`: intercompany fee income and expense
- `1700`: goodwill
- `3300`: translation reserve
- `3400`: non-controlling interest
- `7300`: foreign exchange gains and losses

## `map_uk.csv`: from UK codes to group codes
```
local_code, local_name, group_code
```
It's a lookup. For example, `4000 Sales` points to group `4100 Revenue`, and `7000 Gross wages` points to `6100 Staff costs`. Every account in `tb_uk.csv` has a row here, so none is missing.

## Three things to notice

**1. One mapping is wrong, and the TB won't tell you.**
Find `2310 Deferred income`. It points to group **`4100`, Revenue**. In the group COA, deferred income is `2300`, a liability. The UK holds 180,000 of it, and mapped as written:
- revenue is overstated by 180,000
- group profit is overstated by 180,000
- liabilities are understated by 180,000

The books still **balance**, because the money just moved from one account to another. This is a mistake a "does it balance?" check never catches. You catch it by checking that an account's **nature** matches where it lands. A liability named "deferred income" landing in a revenue account is a contradiction.

**2. The same numbers mean different things in the two systems.**
Compare `map_uk.csv` with the group list:
- UK `1100` is debtors, so it maps to group `1200`.
- UK `1200` is a bank account, so it maps to group `1100`.

The codes are swapped, so you can never assume a local code equals the same group code. The mapping file is the only source of truth.

**3. One mapping row has no data behind it.**
`7920 Exchange differences` maps to group `7300`, but the UK TB has no row for 7920. That's not an error. It's the account where the UK's currency revaluation gain or loss will land later. Just remember it exists.

## Where the AI fits
This is the first real place an LLM could help. A person (or model) reading "Deferred income → Revenue" sees at once that it looks wrong. Code can catch it with a simple rule, such as "a liability-looking name mapped to a revenue account". The model's best use is suggesting the correct mapping with a reason. The decision to apply it should still be checked by a rule or a human.

Think of it as the **menu** every account ends up on. Each row is one account, and each column tells you one fact about it.

## The columns
```
account_code, account_name, account_type, statement, cash_flow_category, normal_balance
```

| Column | What it tells you | Example row |
|---|---|---|
| `account_code` | The account's number | `1200` |
| `account_name` | What it's called | Trade receivables |
| `account_type` | Asset, Liability, Equity, Revenue or Expense | Asset |
| `statement` | Which report it appears on: `BS` or `PL` | BS |
| `normal_balance` | The side it normally sits on | Debit |
| `cash_flow_category` | Not needed for this task. Ignore | Operating |

So `1200,Trade receivables,Asset,BS,Operating,Debit` reads as: "Account 1200 is trade receivables. It's an asset, appears on the balance sheet, and normally has a debit balance."

## The code numbers follow a pattern
You can tell an account's type from its first digit:

| Code starts with | Type | Reports on |
|---|---|---|
| **1**xxx | Assets | Balance sheet |
| **2**xxx | Liabilities | Balance sheet |
| **3**xxx | Equity | Balance sheet |
| **4**xxx | Revenue | P&L |
| **5**xxx to **8**xxx | Expenses | P&L |

For example, `1100` cash, `2100` trade payables, `3100` share capital, `4100` revenue, `6100` staff costs.

## How you'll use it
1. **Where does it go?** Look at `statement`. `BS` accounts build the balance sheet, `PL` accounts build the profit and loss.
2. **Which side should it be?** `normal_balance` tells you what to expect. If an account normally has a credit balance and shows up as a debit, something is unusual and worth checking.
3. **Is a mapping sensible?** This is how you'd catch the deferred income mistake. Group `4100` is `Revenue`, type Revenue. UK's "Deferred income" is a liability, so it doesn't belong there. The mapping check compares the nature of the local account to the type of the group account it lands in.

| Code | Why it's special |
|---|---|
| `1510` accumulated depreciation | An asset type, but its normal balance is **Credit**. It's the contra account we saw in the US file. |

| `4200` / `6300` | Intercompany fee income / expense. They also get eliminated. |
| `1700` goodwill | Created by the India acquisition. |
| `3300` translation reserve | Where currency translation differences go. |
| `3400` non-controlling interest | The 20% India owners' share. |
| `7300` FX gains and losses | An expense account. A loss is a debit, and a gain would be a credit. |

# CLAUDE (12)

Here's the idea in one sentence: **convert all three files into one common shape, point each row at a group account, then add up rows that share a group account.**

## Step 1: put every file into the same shape
Right now the three files look different. We turn each row into one standard record:

```
entity | local code | group code | amount (signed, local currency) | source file + row
```

The amount uses **one sign rule**: debit is positive and credit is negative, which is what the UK file already does.

| Source | How it's converted |
|---|---|
| **US** | Debit and credit columns. Amount = debit − credit. |
| **UK** | Already signed. Use as is. |
| **India** | Amount with a Dr/Cr label. Dr stays positive and Cr becomes negative. |

Every record keeps its **source file and row number**. That's the traceability the brief asks for. An auditor can later follow any figure back to the original line.

## Step 2: find the group account for each row

| Entity | Mapping source |
|---|---|
| **US** | No map file. US codes already are group codes. Check each code exists in `group_coa.csv`. |
| **UK** | Look up `local_code` in `map_uk.csv` |
| **India** | Look up `ledger_code` in `map_in.csv` |

For the US, "no map needed" is an assumption. It's backed by `entities.csv` and a note in `adjustments.json`, but the code should still check every US code against the group COA and report any that doesn't match.

Examples of what happens:

| Source row | Mapped to |
|---|---|
| UK `4000 Sales` −9,850,000 | `4100 Revenue` |
| UK `1200 Bank - Barclays` 1,240,000 | `1100 Cash` |
| UK `7000 Gross wages` CC-OPS 812,500 | `6100 Staff costs` |
| UK `7000 Gross wages` CC-SALES 812,500 | `6100 Staff costs` |
| India `IN-REV` 642,000,000 Cr, so −642,000,000 | `4100 Revenue` |
| US `4100` | `4100` (same) |

## Step 3: add up rows with the same group account
Within each entity, sum all records that share a group code. The two UK wage rows become one `6100` line of 1,625,000, and the record keeps pointers to both source rows. The result is a **TB in group accounts**, one per entity, still in its own currency:

```
entity | group code | amount (local currency) | source rows
UK     | 6100       | 1,625,000               | tb_uk.csv rows 17, 18
```

Only after this do we translate to GBP and combine the entities. That's the next topic.

## Step 4: checks before moving on
The mapping step is where wrong answers can slip in unnoticed, so the code should check:
- **Every row got a mapping.** Any unmapped code is reported, never silently dropped.
- **Totals are preserved.** Each entity's total debits equal its total credits both before and after mapping. If they don't, something was lost or doubled.
- **Mapped accounts make sense.** The account's nature should match the group account type. This is what would catch the UK deferred income row.
- **No duplicates went missing.** The two wage rows must both survive.

## Where the work is
Nothing here needs an LLM. It's lookups and sums. The judgment is in the exceptions: the wrong mapping, the missing mapping, and the US assumption. Those go in the issues report with what the system did about each.

# CLAUDE (15)

Your instinct is right on two points: it **is** credit-side, and it **will** become income eventually. The missing piece is **when**.

## The timing example
A customer pays you £100 in December for a service you'll deliver in January.

- **In December:** you have the cash (debit £100), but you haven't earned it. If the customer cancelled, you'd owe the money back. So you owe either the service or a refund, and that's a **liability** (credit, deferred income).
- **In January:** you deliver the service. Now it's earned, so you move it out of deferred income and into **revenue**.

The credit side doesn't separate the two, because liabilities and revenue are both credit-side. What separates them is whether the work has been done **in this period**.

## Why it matters here
The group reports for the year ended 31 December 2024. The UK's 180,000 is deferred income at that date. That means the work hasn't been done yet, so it belongs to **2025**.

| | Mapped to Revenue (as the file says) | Mapped to Deferred income (correct) |
|---|---|---|
| 2024 revenue | overstated by 180,000 | correct |
| 2024 profit | overstated by 180,000 | correct |
| Liabilities | understated by 180,000 | correct |

A CFO would be signing off profit that includes revenue from work not yet delivered. That's the kind of "looks right but is wrong" error the brief warns about.

## Step 1: how to read `fx_rates.csv`
```
base_currency, quote_currency, rate_type, rate, as_of, convention
```

Take the row `GBP, USD, closing, 1.2530, 2024-12-31, USD per 1 GBP`. It means **£1 = $1.2530** on 31 December 2024.

The file has five kinds of rate. Each is used for a different job:

| Rate type | What it is | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| **closing** | the rate on 31 Dec 2024 | assets and liabilities |
| **average** | the average over FY2024 | US income and expenses |
| **h2_average** | the average for July–Dec 2024 | India income and expenses |
| **spot** | the rate on 1 July 2024 | the day India was bought |
| **opening** | the rate on 31 Dec 2023 | start of the year |

You'll see only GBP/USD and USD/INR directly. There's no GBP/INR row, so you build it: **GBP/INR = GBP/USD × USD/INR**, as `group_policies.md` says. For the closing rate, that's 1.2530 × 85.62 = **107.28 INR per £1**.

There's also a GBP/SGD pair with only an opening and an average rate. **No closing rate for SGD**, which is why that bank figure can't be restated.

## Step 2: how to convert a number
The quote says "USD per 1 GBP", so to go from USD to GBP you **divide**. Multiplying is the common mistake.

| Example | Maths | Result |
|---|---|---|
| US cash, 4,875,000 USD, at closing | 4,875,000 ÷ 1.2530 | **£3,890,662.41** |
| US revenue, 18,400,000 USD, at FY average | 18,400,000 ÷ 1.2780 | **£14,397,496.09** |
| India cash, 285,000,000 INR, at closing | 285,000,000 ÷ 107.28186 | **£2,656,553.49** |
| India July–Dec profit, 42,000,000 INR, at H2 average | 42,000,000 ÷ 107.7918 | **£389,640.03** |

Sanity check: a dollar is worth less than a pound, so the GBP figure is smaller than the USD figure. If your result is bigger, you multiplied instead of dividing.

## Step 3: why it's needed to use different rates
Read policy 2 in `group_policies.md`. It says:
- **Assets and liabilities** use the closing rate.
- **Income and expenses** use the average rate for the period they belong to the group.
- **Equity** uses historical rates.

The reason is that a balance sheet is a snapshot at the year end, so it uses the year-end rate. A P&L is spread over the year, so an average is fairer than picking one day. Equity was put in at a past date and shouldn't be revalued.

The problem is that three different rates make the translated balance sheet **no longer balance**. The gap is real, and policy says it goes to the **translation reserve (account 3300)**. ## The idea
The US charged the UK a management fee. The US records it as **income**, and the UK records it as an **expense**. Inside the group it's money moving from one pocket to another, not real revenue and not a real cost.

If we leave both in:
- group revenue is overstated by the fee
- group expenses are overstated by the same fee
- profit looks unaffected, but revenue and costs are both inflated

So we **eliminate both**. Policy 5 says "eliminated in full".

**US side: the fee income.**
`tb_us.csv` row `4200` shows 640,000 USD. Income is translated at the **average rate** (policy 2). For the US that's the FY2024 average, 1.2780:

| **Total** | **10,074.75** ✓ |

If we eliminated the two as they stand, the UK's real cost for the fifth invoice (8,108.54) would stay in the group's expenses. The group would still show a management fee cost that the group paid to itself, and the receivable and payable on the balance sheet wouldn't tie up either.

**An elimination entry must balance.**
Debits must equal credits, like any entry. Debiting 500,782.47 and crediting 490,707.72 is out by 10,074.75. Something has to absorb the difference, and the right answer is to fix the UK side first (add the in-transit invoice) and then let the leftover be a visible, labelled difference.

## 2. Why does the 1,966.21 go to 7300 and not 4100 revenue?
**4100 is revenue from customers outside the group.** The 1,966.21 isn't a sale to anyone. It's purely an artefact of the exchange rates, since the two sides translated the same invoices at different rates. Putting it in revenue would inflate the control figure `group_revenue` with something that never happened.

7300 is the group's account for exchange differences, and that's where policy 5 sends it. The group reports a gain or loss from currency movement there, and a reader of the statements can see it.

A good test: **the elimination should not change group profit.** Removing the income lowers profit by 500,782.47 and removing the expense raises it by 498,816.26, so profit falls by 1,966.21. The 7300 entry puts that 1,966.21 back, so the net effect on profit is zero. Eliminating internal transactions shouldn't create or destroy profit, so the plug sits in the FX account rather than in revenue.

The US is the parent, so it has no ownership percentage. Use this file as your source of truth. The brief's PDF table is garbled when extracted, but this file is clear.

## `acquisition_note.md`: what happened on 1 July 2024
- The parent bought **80%** of India's shares.
- It paid **INR 690,000,000** in cash.
- India's **net assets at completion** were INR 678,000,000, made up of share capital 250M, reserves at 1 April 410M, and profit for April to June 18M.
- Fair values equal book values, so no adjustments are needed.

You've seen two of those numbers already: the 250M and 410M are in `tb_in.csv`, and the 18M is what April to June added up to in the monthly file.

## Net assets
**Net assets** = assets minus liabilities = the company's equity. If India were sold at book value, 678M is what the owners would get. It's the benchmark to compare the price against.

## Goodwill: paying more than the assets are worth
The parent bought 80%, so it got 80% of the net assets:
80% × 678,000,000 = **542,400,000**

It paid **690,000,000**. The extra is **goodwill**:
690,000,000 − 542,400,000 = **INR 147,600,000**

Goodwill is what you pay for things that aren't on the balance sheet, like the brand, customers and future prospects. It appears as an asset (group account `1700`).

Policy 4 says goodwill is held in the subsidiary's currency (INR) and **retranslated at the closing rate**:
147,600,000 ÷ 107.28186 = **£1,375,815.07**

## Non-controlling interest (NCI): the other 20%
The group consolidates **all** of India's numbers, even though it owns 80%. The other 20% belongs to outside owners. They're shown separately as NCI (account `3400`).

Policy 4: NCI is measured at its **proportionate share of net assets**:
20% × 678,000,000 = **INR 135,600,000** at completion

"Proportionate" means NCI gets only its share of the net assets, with no goodwill allocated to it. That's why all 147.6M of goodwill belongs to the group's side.

NCI then grows each year by 20% of India's profit after the acquisition and by its share of currency translation differences.

## Why only July to December counts
The 18M profit from April to June was earned **before** the group owned India. It's already inside the 678M that was bought, so it can't also count as group profit. That's why we use only the 42M for July to December: 60M for the nine months minus 18M.

## The consolidation entry on day one
In India's currency, on the acquisition date, the group cancels the parent's investment against India's equity:

| Account | Debit | Credit |
|---|---|---|
| Share capital (India) | 250,000,000 | |
| Reserves incl. Apr–Jun profit | 428,000,000 | |
| Goodwill | 147,600,000 | |
| Investment in India (parent's books) | | 690,000,000 |
| Non-controlling interest | | 135,600,000 |
| **Totals** | **825,600,000** | **825,600,000** ✓ |

India's own equity is eliminated because inside the group you can't own yourself, and the parent's investment is eliminated for the same reason. What's left is goodwill and NCI.

## One thing to notice
The parent booked the investment in USD at the 1 July spot rate: 690,000,000 ÷ 83.39 = 8,274,373.43 USD. That figure is in `tb_us.csv` row `1610`. To compare it with India's equity, both need the same currency, and the leftover currency differences go through the translation reserve. That's the last big piece, coming after we look at the opening equity file.

NCI is zero because India hadn't been bought yet. This is the starting point for the statement of changes in equity: opening equity, plus the year's profit, plus the translation movement, plus the India NCI, equals closing equity.

## A check I ran: the opening equity ties exactly
I wanted to see whether the numbers in this file agree with the trial balances, because if they didn't, we'd have another trap. They do:

| Piece | GBP |
|---|---|
| US opening net assets: 16,069,373.43 USD ÷ 1.2730 (opening rate) | 12,623,231.29 |
| plus UK equity: 1,000,000 + 1,641,510 | 2,641,510.00 |
| minus the US's investment in the UK: 1,270,000 USD ÷ 1.2730 | −997,643.36 |
| **Total** | **14,267,097.93** |

That equals the file's total to the penny. Two useful things follow:
- The data is internally consistent, so we can trust `prior_year_group.csv` as a starting point.
- It shows the UK investment is already netted off against UK equity in the opening position, so there's no UK goodwill to calculate. That settles one of my earlier open questions: the UK acquisition (2016) is history, and we just keep eliminating the investment.

## What the translation reserve is made of
The reserve collects every difference caused by translating at different rates. For this year there are three sources:

**1. The US's opening net assets.**
The US starts the year with 16,069,373.43 USD of net assets. At the opening rate that was £12,623,231.29. At the closing rate it's worth £12,824,719.42. That's a **gain of £201,488.13**, because the dollar strengthened against the pound (1.2730 → 1.2530 USD per £, fewer dollars needed for £1).

**2. The US's profit for the year.**
Profit is translated at the average rate, but it also sits in the balance sheet at the closing rate. The gap between the two is a difference.

**3. India, from 1 July.**
India's net assets at acquisition and its July to December profit are translated at different rates (spot, H2 average, closing). The goodwill is also retranslated, from the spot rate to the closing rate. Each creates a difference.

The UK causes **no** difference, because it's already in GBP.

One subtlety: India's differences are shared. The group owns 80%, so only 80% goes to the group's translation reserve and 20% goes to NCI. The opening reserve line says "attributable to owners of the parent", which hints at this split.

## When we calculate it
The movement in the translation reserve can't be finalised yet, because it depends on the final profit, and that depends on which journals we post. We'll do it after the journals, using **two independent routes**:
1. **By components:** add up the three sources above.
2. **By balance:** translate every balance sheet line, and whatever doesn't balance is the reserve.

If the two agree, that's strong evidence nothing was missed, and that's the kind of independent recomputation the brief asks for. If they disagree, we have an error somewhere.

## What it is
A trial balance shows one line for "customers owe us 3,120,000". That line is a **control account**, a total. Behind it is a **sub-ledger**, the detailed list of every customer and how much each owes. The two **must agree**, because the total is just the sum of the list.

`subledger_controls.csv` gives the sub-ledger totals. We compare them with the trial balance:

| Entity | Item | Sub-ledger | Trial balance | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US | Receivables | 3,120,000 | 3,120,000 | 0 |
| US | Payables | 1,665,000 | 1,665,000 | 0 |
| **UK** | **Receivables** | **1,940,000** | **1,985,000** | **45,000** |
| **UK** | **Payables** | **1,165,000** | **1,210,000** | **45,000** |
| India | Receivables | 236,000,000 | 236,000,000 | 0 |
| India | Payables | 168,000,000 | 168,000,000 | 0 |

Only the UK disagrees. The UK trial balance is **45,000 higher than its sub-ledger on both receivables and payables**.

## What it could mean
The same amount on both sides is a clue, but not proof. One possibility is a **set-off**: a customer who is also a supplier, with 45,000 owed each way, netted in the sub-ledger but shown gross in the TB. Another is a posting error. I can't tell from the data, and neither should the code guess.

Here's what each possibility would mean for the statements:
- If it's a gross-up, total assets and total liabilities are both overstated by 45,000 and profit isn't affected.
- If it's an error, the effect depends on which side is wrong.

## What the system should do
Don't adjust the TB, and don't pick a side. The brief says never to fill a gap with a value that isn't in the inputs, and nothing here tells us which figure is correct. So the system should:
1. detect it (a check that compares every control with its sub-ledger, with zero tolerance)
2. record it in `issues.json`: file, the two figures, the 45,000 amount, and what was done (flagged, not adjusted)
3. note the possible effect on total assets so a reviewer knows what to ask

This is a good example of an honest "flagged" outcome rather than a confident guess.

CFOs need statements they can sign, so every number must be right and every number
must trace back to source data.

agree, currencies, minority owners, and data you cannot trust.

=== group_policies.md
# Northwind Group - accounting policies for consolidation (FY2024)

1. **Presentation currency.** The group presents its consolidated statements in GBP.
2. **Translation of entity statements into GBP.**
   - Assets and liabilities: closing rate at 31 December 2024.
   - Income and expenses: average rate for the period in which they are included in the group.
     For the US, the FY2024 average. For India, the H2 (1 July to 31 December 2024) average.
   - Equity: historical rates. Opening group equity is given in `prior_year_group.csv`.
   - Exchange differences on translation go to the translation reserve (account 3300).
   - Where a GBP rate is not given directly, use the product of the two given rates of the same type
     (for example, GBP/INR closing = GBP/USD closing x USD/INR closing).
3. **Foreign currency items inside an entity's own books.** Monetary items in a currency other than the
   entity's functional currency are retranslated at the closing rate. Differences go to profit or loss
   (group account 7300).
4. **Business combinations.** Non-controlling interest is measured at its proportionate share of net assets.
   Goodwill is held in the subsidiary's functional currency and retranslated at the closing rate.

=== group_policies.md
# Northwind Group - accounting policies for consolidation (FY2024)

1. **Presentation currency.** The group presents its consolidated statements in GBP.
2. **Translation of entity statements into GBP.**
   - Assets and liabilities: closing rate at 31 December 2024.
   - Income and expenses: average rate for the period in which they are included in the group.
     For the US, the FY2024 average. For India, the H2 (1 July to 31 December 2024) average.
   - Equity: historical rates. Opening group equity is given in `prior_year_group.csv`.
   - Exchange differences on translation go to the translation reserve (account 3300).
   - Where a GBP rate is not given directly, use the product of the two given rates of the same type
     (for example, GBP/INR closing = GBP/USD closing x USD/INR closing).
3. **Foreign currency items inside an entity's own books.** Monetary items in a currency other than the
   entity's functional currency are retranslated at the closing rate. Differences go to profit or loss
   (group account 7300).
4. **Business combinations.** Non-controlling interest is measured at its proportionate share of net assets.
   Goodwill is held in the subsidiary's functional currency and retranslated at the closing rate.
5. **Intercompany.** Intercompany balances, income and expenses are eliminated in full. Items in transit
   at the year end are recorded by the receiving entity at the closing rate. Any remaining exchange

I've read the brief, all of `context 1.md` and the raw data files. I also re-checked Claude's findings against the data, and they hold up. I didn't read `context 2.md` because you only pointed me at the first one.

## The brief
- **Judgment is the grade.** "What you refused to guess" outweighs the numbers.
- **The six deliverables are all required.** The architecture doc (max 6 pages) is the main artifact.
- **The live session changes an input.** They ask what you expect before you run it, so the pipeline has to be fully explainable.
- **The brief lists what will hurt you.** That includes untraceable figures, invented values, a 12-agent design, and a "send the TB to a model" design.

## What the benchmark Claude actually did
Claude's catches came from four different kinds of reasoning, and the harness has to cover each kind:

| Kind | Examples from the chat | Harness equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| **Mechanical** | unbalanced JE-006, JE-017 dated 2025, the 7000 wage rows being legitimate | deterministic validators |
| **Cross-file tie-outs** | prior-year equity matches US plus UK equity (to the penny), India monthly P&L ties to the TB, April–June profit equals the 18M in the acquisition note, intercompany causes sum to the gap | an invariant library, run as hard gates |
| **Semantic** | deferred income mapped to revenue, JE-014/019 duplicates, JE-009 reversing more than the accrual balance, the injected memo | rules where possible, otherwise an LLM that only proposes, with code deciding |
| **Absence** | no SGD closing rate, `IN-GST-ITC` missing from the mapping, no GBP/INR rate | explicit required-input checks that return `null` plus a reason |

Claude held all of this in one long conversation. The harness has to hold it in structured state: typed findings, each carrying evidence rows. An untyped chat transcript won't do that job.

## Traps in the data that the chat didn't state
1. **Journals use each entity's own codes, so the mapping trap also hits journals.**
   - JE-010 posts to UK `7100`, which is rent (group 6200), but group `7100` is finance costs.
   - JE-011 posts to UK `1100`, which is debtors, but group `1100` is cash.
   - Journals must go through `map_uk` and `map_in` before they are posted.
2. **The sub-ledger check depends on journal state.**
   - JE-011 credits UK debtors by 9,400, which changes the 45,000 gap.
   - Posting JE-016 would break India's AP match (168M).
   - The check should run on the unadjusted TB, with drift reported after journals.
3. **JE-009 is not rescued by ordering.** Even after JE-007 adds 6,800, the accrual is 48,300, which is still below 64,000.
4. **`total_assets` depends on the missing SGD rate.**
   - The brief's appendix says to state in `issues.json` how a missing input was treated.
   - So `sgd_bank_gbp` is `null`. The 23,010 stays at its booked value in `total_assets`, flagged as provisional.
5. **JE-017 could be a hold.** An adjusting-event argument exists, so reject versus hold is a judgment call to document. The same applies to which of JE-014 and JE-019 survives.
6. **JE-018 and JE-020 are unproven.** I'd post them, but the overlap with India's monthly P&L is an open question.

## The harness
- **Detector registry.** Each trap class becomes a registered detector that emits a typed issue (file, row, amount, action taken).
- **Invariants as blocking gates.** Every tie-out above is coded as a gate. A failed gate halts or escalates; nothing gets plugged.
- **A narrow LLM role.** It only handles the semantic residue and returns structured proposals with cited rows. It sees data as quoted data and has no authority to change a status.
- **A "does it match the nature of the account" check.** This is the one that would catch deferred income, because the TB balances either way.
- **An adversarial-fixtures test.** Plant new traps and confirm the harness finds them, since they will change an input live.

## Open items
- **Deadline.** Your files are dated 21 Oct, but today is 16 Nov. Is the 7-day clock already running or does it start now?
- **Company name.** The brief says Plainflow, not Inteegrate.
- **Clarifying emails.** You have three. Two good ones are whether the journals are already in the TBs, and how to eliminate the investment in the UK.

Want me to read `context 2.md` next, or move straight to the architecture?
